title: The 76ers' Tacko Fall Gambit Is Desperation Dressed As Depth
author: Doc
summary: Converting an injured 7-6 novelty who hasn't played NBA basketball in four years isn't a solution—it's a symptom of a bigger problem.

content.value:
## This Is What Cap-Induced Panic Looks Like

The 76ers converted Tacko Fall to a two-way contract after reserve center Ariel Hukporti tore his Achilles in the team's preseason opener, and the move tells you everything about Philadelphia's self-inflicted roster crisis. The Sixers sit just $1.8 million below the first apron, which means they cannot sign a player to replace Hukporti without either waiving someone or making a small trade. So instead of acquiring functional NBA depth, they're keeping a 30-year-old who did not play during the preseason because of a hip strain sustained during a training camp practice and has played in 37 career NBA games with Boston and Cleveland, but none since the 2021-22 season.

This isn't roster construction—it's making the best of a bad situation while pretending you're adding a real asset. The move provides insurance, experience and a unique skill set as the Sixers round out their roster, according to the team's spin, but insurance is only useful when it can actually be deployed. Fall has already been sidelined for weeks, and even when healthy, there's no recent evidence he belongs on an NBA floor in meaningful minutes.

## The Numbers Don't Support the Nostalgia

Fall's NBA career amounts to 37 games spread across three seasons, all in mop-up duty. His playing time overseas is the only thing keeping this conversation alive, but context matters. He spent the 2025-26 campaign with the Ningbo Rockets, averaging 11.2 points and 6.0 rebounds in 38 games in the Chinese Basketball Association—a league where his size advantage is magnified and the defensive schemes bear little resemblance to what he'll face in the NBA.

The Sixers are banking on the idea that someone who shot 80 percent from the field against weaker international competition can translate those skills back to a league that exposed his limitations years ago. Fall played in 37 career NBA games, and his shooting percentage in those games was solid, but he averaged just 2.2 points and 2.4 rebounds across those appearances. He wasn't a rotation player then, and four years removed from the league, with a current hip injury, he's not going to become one now.

What Fall brings is spectacle, not substance. He'll generate fan excitement when the Sixers are up 25 in garbage time, but that's not what a team with championship aspirations should be optimizing for on their depth chart.

## The Real Problem Is the Frontcourt Void

The Fall signing is a symptom, not the disease. The Sixers are also without the last remaining center on the roster, Adem Bona, who has yet to participate in training camp due to a left foot sprain, and their remaining options include Jabari Walker, Dean Wade and Dominick Barlow, although none offers the same combination of size and traditional center skills. Philadelphia constructed a roster with Joel Embiid as the centerpiece, then failed to adequately insure that centerpiece with competent backup big men.

Fall joins Caleb Love and Rayan Rupert as the team's three two-way players, which means Philadelphia is using one of its limited developmental slots on someone who isn't developing—he's 30 years old and has already peaked. The Sixers could have used that spot on a younger player with actual upside, or structured their offseason differently to preserve cap flexibility for exactly this kind of emergency.

Instead, they're now in a position where converting an injured center who last played NBA basketball during the 2021-22 season qualifies as addressing a need. That's not clever roster management. That's what happens when you paint yourself into a financial corner and hope goodwill and nostalgia can paper over the structural flaws.

## Size Alone Doesn't Solve Matchup Problems

The argument for Fall rests almost entirely on his height. At 7-foot-6, he's a matchup nightmare in theory—someone who can alter shots and provide rim protection without jumping. But the NBA figured out years ago that Fall's lack of lateral mobility makes him unplayable in most defensive schemes, and his offensive game offers nothing beyond putbacks and lobs. The move makes sense given the team's need for frontcourt depth, and Fall brings a unique combination of size and rim protection, but uniqueness is only valuable if it translates to winning basketball.

Philadelphia's frontcourt problems demand real solutions, not publicity stunts masquerading as depth additions. The Sixers need someone who can credibly defend pick-and-rolls, survive switches, and hold down minutes when Embiid sits or misses games. Fall checks none of those boxes. What he does check is the "emergency break glass in case of complete roster collapse" box, which is exactly where the Sixers find themselves after Hukporti's injury and Bona's continued absence.

Converting Fall to a two-way deal isn't the worst move Philadelphia could make given their constraints, but it's a reminder that those constraints were self-imposed. When your backup plan is a player who hasn't seen NBA action in four years and can't get on the court due to injury, you don't have a backup plan—you have a hope and a prayer.
